questions.prompt: Skeletal muscle fibres are multinucleated cells formed by the fusion of many individual cells.
The sarcomere is defined as the region between two adjacent M lines within a myofibril.
Thick filaments are primarily composed of the protein myosin.
Troponin C initiates contraction by binding to sodium ions in the sarcoplasm.
The A band represents the region of the sarcomere that contains only thick filaments and never overlaps with thin filaments.
Transverse tubules (T tubules) are invaginations of the sarcolemma that allow action potentials to reach the interior of the muscle fiber.
Acetylcholine is the endogenous neurotransmitter used to initiate contraction at the somatic neuromuscular junction.
Smooth muscle is characterized by the presence of sarcomeres arranged in highly regular, parallel arrays.
The sarcoplasmic reticulum acts as the primary storage organelle for intracellular calcium in skeletal muscle fibers.
The binding of a new ATP molecule to the myosin head causes the dissociation of the actomyosin complex.
In a single muscle twitch, the duration of the mechanical response is significantly longer than the duration of the exciting action potential.
Gap junctions are essential for the electrical coupling of cardiac myocytes, allowing the heart to function as a syncytium.
Multi-unit smooth muscle behaves as a syncytium because its cells are interconnected by numerous low-resistance gap junctions.
Tropomyosin functions as a regulatory protein that covers myosin-binding sites on actin when a muscle is at rest.
Fast-glycolytic (Type IIb/IIx) muscle fibers contain a higher concentration of myoglobin than slow-oxidative (Type I) fibers.
Calcium ions trigger smooth muscle contraction by binding to calmodulin, which then activates myosin light chain kinase.
The power stroke of the cross-bridge cycle is directly triggered by the hydrolysis of ATP into ADP and P_i.
An isotonic contraction occurs when the muscle shortens while lifting a constant load.
Frequency summation occurs when a second action potential stimulates a twitch before the first twitch has fully subsided.
Skeletal muscle contraction is entirely dependent on the influx of extracellular calcium through L-type calcium channels.
The plateau phase of the cardiac action potential is primarily maintained by a prolonged inward calcium current.
Maximum active tension is developed when a sarcomere is stretched to its maximum length, minimizing filament overlap.
Unitary smooth muscle is the predominant muscle type found in the walls of the gastrointestinal tract and bladder.
Acetylcholinesterase is synthesized in the presynaptic terminal to facilitate the rapid synthesis of new acetylcholine molecules.
Relaxation in smooth muscle requires the enzyme myosin light chain phosphatase to remove phosphate groups from the regulatory light chain.
The I band of a sarcomere increases in length as the muscle contracts and filaments overlap more.
Slow-twitch muscle fibers are characterized by low mitochondrial density and high glycolytic enzyme activity.
Rigor mortis is caused by an excess of ATP, which prevents myosin from detaching from the actin filament.
Skeletal muscle excitation-contraction coupling requires a net influx of extracellular calcium through L-type channels to trigger RyR1.
Dense bodies in smooth muscle are restricted to the inner surface of the cell membrane and are not found within the cytoplasm.
